papers.title: Designing Physics-Informed Quantum Simulations with Qubits and Qudits
papers.abstract: Simulating the real-time dynamics of interacting quantum systems is a long-standing challenge for classical computation. This thesis studies how quantum computers can address this challenge in three settings from nuclear and particle physics: collective neutrino oscillations, low-energy nuclear dynamics, and lattice gauge theories coupled to matter. We examine how the choice of encoding, simulation algorithm, and error-correction strategy affects the resources needed to simulate each system. For collective three-flavour neutrino oscillations, we develop qubit and qutrit circuits and implement them on superconducting quantum processors. We compare their gate requirements and sensitivity to noise, and show that error mitigation yields flavour probabilities in agreement with theoretical predictions for several time steps. For nuclear dynamics described by pionless effective field theory, we formulate the problem in first quantization and derive explicit resource estimates for product-formula and quantum-signal-processing algorithms. In the dilute regime relevant to nuclear scattering, first-quantized methods reduce both logical-qubit and gate requirements relative to second-quantized approaches. Among the methods considered, generalized quantum signal processing gives the lowest estimated gate cost. These time-evolution estimates suggest that low-energy nuclear scattering could be a candidate application for early fault-tolerant quantum computers. Finally, we investigate how the local symmetries of lattice gauge theories can provide part of the redundancy needed for quantum error correction, helping to reduce the additional encoding overhead. For ZN gauge theories with prime N encoded on N-level qudits, we show that Gauss's law defines a code protecting against bit-flip errors. We identify its logical operators with gauge-invariant observables and use them to derive a bosonic dual description. We then extend the construction to qubit encodings of ZN gauge theories with N a power of 2, where the constraints require stabilizers beyond the Pauli group, and show how these constraints can still be used for error correction and gauge fixing. This paves the way to more efficient encodings, and introduces new tools for the study of lattice gauge theories. Together, these results show how physical structure can guide the choice of encodings, algorithms, and error-correction schemes for more resource-efficient quantum simulation.

papers.title: Towards Semi-Automatic Benchmarking of Large Language Models for Self-Regulated Language Learning
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular personal assistants for language learning purposes. While exhibiting impressive capabilities on various Natural Language Processing tasks, including text summarisation, paraphrase generation, and question answering, their capacity to provide language learners with pedagogically adequate feedback is less clear. This is due, among other causes, to the lack of annotated data. In this paper, we describe a framework which aims at bridging this gap by (i) collecting manually annotated LLM-generated answers to learners' queries, and (ii) using this data to automatically characterise LLM skills along pedagogical dimensions with respect to a taxonomy of self-regulated LLM uses by language learners. This framework has been used to assess the ability of contemporary mainstream LLMs to generate pedagogically adequate answers to L2 French learners. Preliminary results on a small manually annotated dataset (N = 49) show that establishing a definitive assessment of these models remains elusive; rather, they reveal an absence of consensus among human experts when evaluating models.

papers.title: With a Little Help From AI?! Governing Visual Hate Speech Through AI-Assisted Counter-Image Practices
papers.abstract: The attention-grabbing and memorable nature of visuals makes them a powerful vehicle for spreading hate online. As platforms increasingly reconsider or scale back content moderation efforts, user-centered interventions are gaining importance as complementary governance strategies. While prior research demonstrates the effectiveness of empathy-based textual counter speech, little is known about the role of visual counter speech in mitigating hateful imagery. This preregistered study examines the effectiveness of user-centered interventions against visual hate speech. Using an experimental design (N = 666), we tested four interventions against a no-intervention control condition in response to hateful images targeting transgender persons: (a) empathy-based textual counter speech, (b) AI-generated generic counter images, (c) AI-generated specific counter images replicating elements of the original, and (d) platform-issued warning labels. Results show substantial variation across interventions. Empathy-based textual counter speech and AI-generated specific counter images showed the most consistent reductions in amplification-oriented behaviors, particularly forwarding. Visual interventions did not outperform textual counter speech, suggesting that effectiveness depends less on modality and more on the specificity and contextual alignment of the intervention. Furthermore, effectiveness varied with the intensity of the hate content. Interventions were most effective for humor-based, more ambiguously harmful content, whereas their impact diminished for more severe forms of hate. The consistent performance of AI-generated specific counter images further points to the potential of generative AI to provide users with a rapid, low-cost, and accessible means of producing context-sensitive counter speech.

papers.title: Combining PageRank Modularization and Ontology Verbalization for LLM-Based Complex Ontology Matching
papers.abstract: Complex matching remains a challenge in the ontology matching field. Existing approaches are constrained by strong assumptions on their input: instance-based and rule-mining systems require populated ontologies and reliable links between their instances, while systems built on pre-trained encoders operate at the schema level but target primarily simple correspondences. Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising, yet they either rely on manually built ontology modules or feed formal serializations directly to the model. This paper proposes a schema-only pipeline that addresses these limitations by integrating (i) an automatic modularization strategy combining the PageRank and Personalized PageRank algorithms, which reduces the search space while controlling the specificity of the extracted context; and (ii) a verbalization module that turns ontology modules into natural language descriptions, exploited both for embedding-based candidate generation and as context in LLM prompts. The approach is evaluated on four datasets of the OAEI Complex track. Relying solely on schema-level information, our matcher achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art complex matching systems.

papers.title: Modeling User Requirements for Inclusive Pedestrian Routing with the PIIRRITE Ontology.
papers.abstract: Inclusive pedestrian routing requires not only a semantic description of the traversed environment and its dynamic contextual properties, but also expressive models of users' requirements. Existing ontology-based user profiling approaches primarily organize user characteristics into taxonomies, providing limited support for representing conditional requirements that can be evaluated against changing environmental properties. Conversely, ontologies describing pedestrian environments focus mainly on spatial and contextual information, with little support for modeling the structure and semantics of user requirements. This paper extends the PIIRRITE ontology with two new modelets for representing user requirements, including the accessibility-related ones, in pedestrian routing. Our model captures user profiles as sets of conditional requirements, distinguishes requirement importance from flexibility, supports recursively composed requirements, and introduces a distance factor mechanism for proximity-sensitive constraints. We validate the ontology by instantiating a knowledge graph of the LyonTech La Doua campus with representative user personas, evaluating SPARQL queries implementing a set of competency questions, and computing an inadequacy score quantifying a route's suitability for a given user profile.

papers.title: STAR-Q: A Web-Based Platform for Annotating Qualified Knowledge Graph Statements in Texts and Tables
papers.abstract: The construction and evaluation of knowledge graph (KG) population systems depend on high-quality, entitygrounded annotated corpora. However, producing such corpora remains a laborious task: general-purpose annotation tools do not often support the grounding of annotations to KG identifiers, rarely handle tabular content, and provide little support for corpus-level quality control. In this paper, we present STAR-Q (Span and Table Annotation for RDF with Qualifiers), an open-source, web-based annotation platform designed to facilitate the annotation of both texts and tables with knowledge graph entities. STAR-Q lets users highlight mentions corresponding to subjects, predicates, objects, and ordered qualifier predicate-value pairs directly in documents, and then disambiguate them to entities and properties defined in a reference knowledge graph through a configurable lookup interface targeting any Wikibase instance. Wikidata is supported out of the box, with its large set of QIDs and PIDs. Private Wikibase deployments, such as enterprise knowledge graphs, can also be registered and selected per corpus. Annotations use a unified component schema covering both textual spans and character ranges within table cells; resolved values may be KG resources, corpus-local entities and relations, or typed literals. Beyond annotation, STAR-Q provides corpus management and import adapters for structured JSON/JSONL, archive-based corpus formats, Label Studio exports, and its own versioned full-corpus JSON. Annotations generated by the tool can be exported in RDF 1.2, either in a "truthy" statement mode or in a "full" mode preserving component-level text and table evidence using well-known ontologies (DCAT, PROV, NIF, CSVW, Web Annotations). Wikidata-grounded statements can additionally be exported as QuickStatements 3.0 commands for direct submission to Wikidata. We demonstrate STAR-Q through two scenarios: a didactic scenario based on Wookieepedia texts annotated with Wikidata entities curated by the WikiProject Star Wars community effort, and an industrial in-use scenario, where technical telecommunications documents are annotated against an enterprise knowledge graph. The tool is open source at https://github.com/ecladatta/star-q.

papers.title: Automatically Building and Updating a Knowledge Graph of MLIP Models
papers.abstract: Complementing the many efforts in providing semantic representations of concepts, notions, and entities in materials science, we report and illustrate a process by which we can automatically build a knowledge graph of the fast evolving field of machine learning applied to the prediction of material properties, focusing on MLIP (Machine Learning Interatomic Potential). This LLM-based process relies on multiple steps, from information extraction in documents and articles to a validation loop using SHACL constraints to detect and correct errors. It is carried out on a model-by-model basis, focusing on the consistency of representation, therefore enabling an iterative construction where the addition of new models is facilitated. We illustrate the process by showing a few interesting aspects that can be queried from a knowledge graph built from the models listed in the Matbench Discovery leaderboard.

papers.title: Towards Ontology-Guided and Traceable GraphRAG for Legal Knowledge in Industrial Maintenance
papers.abstract: Regulatory industrial maintenance relies on legal texts that are numerous, evolving, and highly interconnected. GraphRAG extends Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating knowledge graphs (KGs) into retrieval and answer generation, offering a promising approach for exploiting the semantic relationships embedded in texts. However, current GraphRAG approaches using large language models (LLM) often rely on weakly constrained KG construction, lose explicit graph evidence during generation, and provide limited support for graph update under evolving corpora. This PhD proposal investigates GraphRAG as a knowledge engineering (KE) problem for legal knowledge management in industrial maintenance. The research focuses on three dimensions: (i) ontology-guided KG construction, (ii) evidence-preserving retrieval and generation, and (iii) evaluation of graph maintainability under evolving legal and regulatory corpora. Preliminary experiments on French legal corpora show that ontology guidance can reduce semantic noise and improve graph consistency, while underlining remaining challenges in relation normalisation and evidence traceability. Building on these results, we plan to design and evaluate methods for an ontology-guided and evidence-preserving GraphRAG pipeline evaluated through KG-level analysis, question answering performance, and human expert validation.

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs as External Memory for LLM-based Scientific Assistants
papers.abstract: Scientific assistants must remember the questions, observations, parameters, and intermediate results that accumulate across days or weeks of inquiry, and trace each conclusion back to its evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs) lack such a structured, persistent memory, which causes contextual degradation, hallucinations, and excessive cost from overusing the context window. This thesis proposes a neuro-symbolic architecture that couples an LLM-based agent with a knowledge graph (KG) built on standardized formal languages (RDF, RDFS, OWL 2 RL, SHACL, SPARQL) and reusing existing ontologies (e.g. PROV-O) whenever possible. In contrast to state-of-the-art memory systems, which rely on schemaless or proprietary property graphs, our hypothesis is that grounding agent memory in open standards improves the six memory operations (consolidation, indexing, updating, forgetting, retrieval, compression) through formal reasoning and declarative validation, at a latency overhead that stays negligible relative to the LLM call. We present the problem, three research questions and their hypotheses, a first experimental prototype that implements an end-to-end store-and-retrieve pipeline, and an evaluation plan combining the LongMemEval and LoCoMo benchmarks with a test case in metabolomics.

papers.title: Stochastic approximation with delayed updates: Asynchronous Machine Learning Algorithms study
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the convergence dynamics of stochastic approximation algorithms under delayed gradient updates and their impact on asynchronous machine learning performance. We present a comprehensive case study comparing the asymptotic behavior of stochastic gradient descent with theoretical guarantees from stochastic approximation theory, examining both decaying and constant learning rate regimes. For decaying rates, we verify convergence but demonstrate that high delays necessitate impractical learning rates; for constant rates, we show that systematically exploiting the learning rate and delay relationship enables robust asynchronous learning. Furthermore, we identify that popular adaptive optimizers degrade under delays because of estimating curvature at current rather than delayed iterates. Finally, we propose a theoretically grounded Hessian-based correction framework using modified Newton-Raphson iterations that explicitly account for gradient staleness.

papers.abstract: Twenty years ago, a group of Semantic Web researchers set out to do for ontologies what the Gang of Four did for software. This talk retraces that love story, from NeOn and eXtreme Design to WOP, through an analysis of 788 papers. Language models now generate and match patterns, solving what we could not, while the bottleneck moves to trust. I argue that patterns matter more than ever, as the unit linking models, people and knowledge graphs, and outline the challenges ahead.

papers.title: The Agent Internet A New Evolutionary Phase of the Web and Its Global Impact
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) based software agents are transitioning from one shot assistants to long term actors that plan, negotiate and accomplish tasks with multiple services. This transformation is resulting in what researchers call the Agent Internet, the Agentic Web or the Internet of Agents, in which programs are full-fledged players alongside people. This article summarizes academic surveys, industry studies and public market data from 2025 to 2026 to outline the multi-layered nature of this setup and to consider its pros and cons. According to market estimates, the revenue for agent software is estimated to be around eight billion dollars in 2025 and up to 35-53 billion dollars in 2030. Adoption statistics tell a tale of much experimentation and few pilots taking it to scale. We discuss communication protocols that enable agents to find and trust each other, the as yet undeveloped identity and payment layers and the burden of agent traffic on advertising supported content. But the challenges that we see are not just capabilities, but security, accountability, interoperability, and who pays for content and compute. Finally, we highlight some of the current research and policy gaps and suggest avenues for a responsible construction.

papers.title: ModelMatch: A Lightweight Passive Token-based Fingerprinting of LLMs
papers.abstract: The widespread deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) through black-box APIs raises significant trust and compliance concerns, as users lack guarantees that the responding model matches the one advertised. This opacity enables risks such as silent model substitution for cost reduction or Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks that redirect queries to malicious models. papers.title: AgentFlowShield: Defending LLM Agents Against Metadata Side Channels
papers.abstract: Tool-augmented LLM agents produce structured, multi-phase network traffic whose encrypted metadata-packet sizes, inter-arrival times, burst boundaries, and streaming cadence-can reveal which tools were invoked, whether retrieval or memory was used, and coarse properties of the underlying task. We study this leakage in a scoped single-endpoint deployment model and introduce AgentFlowShield, a phase-aware egress shaping layer combining bucket padding, frame aggregation, bounded jitter, tool normalisation, memory envelopes, and a risk-aware controller. On a 6,300-trace controlled testbed we evaluate six inference attacks under no-defence, generic, and phaseaware defences, probe generalisation with a template-disjoint split, and evaluate three defence-aware adversaries. We provide a bounded within-phase size-channel analysis, identify residual leakage channels, and demonstrate the defence architecture in a controlled loopback testbed with synthetic WAN noise. AgentFlowShield-full preserves low engineering overhead (24 % measured latency overhead in the final utility run) but does not eliminate leakage against the strongest standard-split adversaries (97-100% residual AUPRC on A1-A4). Its clearest gains appear in the template-disjoint and policy-aware settings: D9 shows mixed results in unseen-template splits, with workflow-type AUPRC increasing from 0.385 to 0.453 (indicating higher detectability) and tool-type decreasing from 0.512 to 0.490, while policy-aware A1 fusion drops from 0.995 under random padding to 0.442 under D9. The final results therefore show a narrower but more defensible claim: phase-aware shaping helps generalisation-resistant and calibrated attacks, but fixed-envelope defences still leave strong residual standard-split signals.

papers.title: FedWidthKD : Federated Data-Free KD for Width-Heterogeneous DS-CNNs
papers.abstract: Despite the rapid growth of edge computing, deploying collaborative machine learning across heterogeneous devices remains a fundamental challenge in Federated Learning (FL). Existing approaches either assume uniform model architectures across clients or rely on nested subnetworks that may leave parts of the global model insufficiently updated when no full-width client participates. We propose FedWidthKD, a federated learning framework designed to support DS-CNN architectures with heterogeneous client widths. Client models can be narrower than or equal in width to the global model, allowing the server to reconstruct and maintain a full-width model even when no full-width client participates. Our method combines sample-weighted, coverage-normalized aggregation with a warm-up width-expansion procedure that replicates the available channels and applies norm-scaled perturbations to initialize the full-width architecture. We further apply data-free server-side ensemble distillation on procedurally generated inputs to transfer knowledge from the heterogeneous local models to all channels of the global model without using private client data. Experimental results across four image-classification benchmarks show that FedWidthKD is particularly effective under width and statistical heterogeneity. In the heterogeneous-width evaluation, FedWidthKD outperforms the HeteroFL baseline in 22 of 27 comparisons, including 8 of 9 configurations in which no client trains the full-width model.

papers.title: PIIRRITE: An Ontology for Inclusive Itineraries Modeling
papers.abstract: Enabling inclusive pedestrian routing requires capturing users' specific needs and preferences and leveraging environmental characteristics derived from diverse and heterogeneous data sources. In this paper, we introduce PIIRRITE (Pedestrian InclusIve indooR-outdooR ITinerariEs), an ontology designed to serve as a semantic backbone for inclusive pedestrian routing across indoor and outdoor environments. We build on existing domain ontologies such as GeoSPARQL to represent spatial entities and SAREF to attach contextual properties to spatial entities such as accessibility-related characteristics and environmental conditions. Our ontology is developed using the SAMOD methodology through successive modelets driven by a set of competency questions reflecting user requirements. By bringing together heterogeneous spatial and contextual data, the ontology enables querying and reasoning over diverse data sources to support personalized and inclusive itinerary planning. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach through a real-world case study based on the LyonTech La Doua campus.

papers.title: DICF: Domain-Invariant Counterfactual Explanations
papers.abstract: One desired property of counterfactual explanations is plausibility, that is, a resemblance to real-world data. This property can be achieved by constraining counterfactuals lying in the data manifold. Unfortunately, the data often comes from multiple distinct environments (or domains) or changes under distribution shifts. This may alter the counterfactual validity and plausibility. To address this issue, we propose Domain-Invariant Counterfactual Explanations (DICF), a novel self-explaining framework rooted in invariant representation learning. By explicitly disentangling the latent representation into an invariant class space and a domain space, DICF enables counterfactual search within a predictive space, while preserving the domain specificities. We also introduce a dedicated mechanism to learn the distribution of unseen domains. Empirical evaluations on several datasets demonstrate that when the underlying assumption of class and domain independence holds, such as in image data, DICF finds a trade-off between minimizing feature perturbations and maximizing domain preservation. Furthermore, in mixed-type tabular environments, where domain and predictive features are inherently entangled, the framework remains competitive against state-of-theart baselines.

papers.title: Supernetwork Architecture Selection for Deployable Language Models: RAG Assessment of Overhead-Line Insulators on a 2 GB Device for Grid Operator's Maintenance Crews
papers.abstract: Transmission system operators inspecting high-voltage insulator strings using inference using drone capture inference in remote locations need a local LLM assistant that is useful only if its answers are hallucination-free, drawn from operator-held documents and never exceeding what a photograph shows. The assistant presented here is built accordingly, a detector turning photographs into fixed-text findings, retrieval covering 3,780 IEC, CIGRE and IEEE passages and 127 engineer-reviewed question-answer pairs, and code-enforced hallucination guards checking every answer. Because everything runs within the memory restrictions of an edge device such as the 2 GB Arduino UNO Q, the language model must fit the device, so a weight-sharing supernetwork is trained once from Llama 3.2 1B and eleven subnetworks varying in size are extracted and distilled from a Qwen3.5-27B teacher, yielding a deployable model family. Which network is selected is decided by a selection rule, evaluation set and GPT-OSS:20B judge, ranking candidates by answer quality under a hallucination guard gate and memory restrictions. All subnetworks keep guard violations at or below 2.8% and answer the field questions on the device without failure at 2.8 W, the service peaking at 1108 to 1258 MB as quality rises along the memory-quality Pareto frontier from 0.73 to 0.91 and the median 704-token answer lengthens from 79 to 134 s. The shipped network is the fastest of the three tied on quality within 1200 MB, at 0.85, 94 s per answer and 1172 MB.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Marketing
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technologies shaping modern marketing. The rapid growth of digital platforms, customer data, and automated technologies has changed how businesses understand consumers, communicate with audiences, and measure marketing performance. AI enables organizations to analyse large datasets, predict consumer behaviour, personalize communication, automate routine tasks, and generate content. This research paper examines the role of AI in marketing, its major applications, benefits, challenges, ethical concerns, and future implications. The paper argues that AI can significantly improve marketing effectiveness when combined with human creativity, strategic judgment, and responsible data practices. At the same time, concerns regarding privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, transparency, and employment demonstrate the need for careful and ethical implementation. The future of marketing is therefore likely to depend on a collaborative relationship between human marketers and intelligent technologies.

papers.title: Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference Systems: Architecture, Learning, Input Selection, and Applications - A Survey
papers.abstract: Abstract Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) is a hybrid intelligent modeling framework that fuses the linguistic interpretability of fuzzy if-then rules with the parameter-learning capability of artificial neural networks. Since its introduction by Jang in 1993, ANFIS has become one of the most widely adopted neuro-fuzzy architectures for nonlinear function approximation, system identification, and time-series prediction. This paper surveys the ANFIS framework from three complementary angles. First, it reviews the network architecture and the hybrid learning rule that combines gradient descent with least-squares estimation, drawing on Jang's foundational formulation. Second, it examines a practical challenge in applying ANFIS to real-world, high-dimensional problems determining which candidate variables should serve as network inputs and reviews a computationally efficient input-selection heuristic based on single-epoch training error. Third, it presents a case study of ANFIS applied to high-frequency financial trading, in which an event-based volatility model, the Intraday Seasonality Observation Model (ISOM), is used to pre-filter training data and materially improves trading performance metrics such as return on investment and the Sharpe ratio. The paper closes with a comparative discussion of strengths, limitations, and open research directions for neuro-fuzzy modeling.

papers.title: AI Hallucinations
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has really transformed areas like healthcare, legal services, education, finance, and business. But its quick spread also brings persistent tech troubles, mainly the confusing issue of AI mistakes, errors, and misinformation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle all sorts of tasks, from text creation and code writing to answering questions and summarizing info. Still, despite their big achievements, LLMs sometimes spout incorrect stuff – factually wrong or made-up content – which is called "hallucination." This paper dives deep into AI failures, showing how they differ based on errors in logic, generated fiction presented confidently, and correct data being misinterpreted. It looks at why AI systems act overly sure of themselves, how messy training data messes up, and ideas for fixing this like boosted retrieval methods, cleaner training data, and humans checking the work. What stands out is that these glitches aren't just random tech snafus. Instead, they're a design quirk of big AI language models. Fixing them demands teamwork from folks in various fields, not just developers. So, while there are big issues, figuring out ways to collaborate could make these systems way more reliable in the future.

papers.title: Explainable AI in Critical Systems: Techniques, Trust and Challenges
papers.abstract: Abstract In highly sensitive areas like healthcare, cybersecurity, transport and finance, where an unexplainable or incorrect decision could have dire consequences, AI also aids in making decisions. Explainable AI (XAI) has become a widely suggested way to create transparency, accountability and trust, yet the literature is scattered both by technique, domain and evaluation methods. A focused critical review of 14 studies published from 2020 to 2026 is presented, consisting of 11 surveys and systematic reviews, 2 studies that were empirical with an intrusion detection focus and 1 clinician-based evaluation of the heatmap methods. We categorize the various XAI techniques according to scope, timing, model dependence and explanation form, distinguish between the technical trustworthiness of an explanation and the human calibration of trust and combine the evaluation of explanations in practice. The evidence reveals that post-hoc, local methods, in particular SHAP, LIME and Grad-CAM, outstood in terms of applications, explanations have progressed with greater speed than explanation validation, and most of the studies did not focus on quantitative evaluation or user studies, while expert judgements of the plausibility of explanations were not reliably associated with the quality of the models. We argue that explanations in critical systems must be seen as artefacts for safety, which must be validated, and that a research agenda should be pursued in the areas of standardized evaluation, human centered studies, privacy preserving explanation and regulatory alignment.

papers.title: The Voice of AI: Consumer Psychology and the Strategic Use of AI-Generated Voices in Marketing
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is transforming marketing communication, with AI-generated voices emerging as an increasingly important means through which brands communicate with consumers. This paper examines AI-generated voices from a consumer psychology perspective, focusing on how consumers interpret and respond to synthetic voices used in marketing communication. Drawing on literature from artificial intelligence, marketing, consumer behaviour and human–computer interaction, the paper explores the psychological significance of vocal characteristics such as naturalness, human-likeness, prosody, anthropomorphism and emotional expression. It further examines how these characteristics can shape consumer perceptions of message credibility, authenticity and brand trust. The discussion highlights the growing use of AI-generated voices across advertising, social media, voice commerce and interactive brand communication, with selected examples from the Indian marketing context illustrating their applications in personalisation, engagement and localisation. The paper argues that the effectiveness of AI-generated voices depends not simply on technological sophistication, but on how consumers psychologically interpret the voice and its relationship with the message and brand. The paper concludes by identifying directions for future research on AI-mediated brand communication.

papers.abstract: La tecnología de computación cuántica, con su potencia de cálculo exponencialmente superior a la de las computadoras actuales, hace vulnerables los sistemas críticos, como los sistemas de votación electrónica, lo que significará un riesgo potencial para la integridad de la democracia. Este artículo analiza el impacto de la transición a un sistema de votación cuántica. Al examinar la literatura existente y simular protocolos en un entorno cuántico, el estudio evalúa los beneficios y desafíos relacionados con la seguridad, la integridad y la confiabilidad, con el objetivo de proteger los procesos democráticos contra futuras amenazas tecnológicas.

papers.title: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Fashion and Apparel Related Reviews using Transformer Model
papers.abstract: The increasing reliance on e-commerce has led to a surge in customer-generated content, making sentiment analysis a crucial tool for understanding consumer preferences. This study presents a novel aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) approach to extract fine-grained insights from customer reviews across multiple product categories, including lingerie, women’s clothing, men’s clothing, kids’ apparel, home & furniture, and flowers & plants. We employ exploratory data analysis (EDA) to uncover key patterns in customer sentiment and utilize a transformer-based model with contrastive learning to enhance sentiment classification accuracy. Our approach effectively captures sentiment variations across nine different aspects, including quality, value for money, style, fit, material, warmth, comfort, support, and how well the product fits. The results demonstrate that our model outperforms traditional sentiment analysis methods, offering a more structured understanding of customer feedback. By analyzing customer sentiments from reviews, businesses can identify dissatisfaction patterns that may contribute to customer churn. Addressing these issues proactively can help improve customer retention and loyalty. These insights can help businesses refine their product offerings and improve customer satisfaction across diverse e-commerce categories.

papers.title: No Masking Needed: Predicting Latent Semantics for Efficient Pre-training of Encoder-based Language Models
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Latent Semantic Modeling (LSM), a sample-efficient alternative for pre-training encoder-based language models that does not require the use of a special mask symbol. This is beneficial, as it allows us to perform pre-training on naturally occurring sentences (as opposed to such ones that contain an unnatural mask symbol, which symbol is otherwise not included during fine-tuning). The main idea behind LSM is that instead of requiring the language model to return the exact identity of randomly selected (sub)tokens from an input sequence, it determines their latent semantic properties extracted from an auxiliary model using sparse coding over its activations. When fine-tuned for downstream applications, models pre-trained with LSM often perform as good or better as alternatively pre-trained models that use considerably more compute per update steps and which have gone through considerably more pre-training steps, illustrating the improved representation developed during LSM pre-training. We release our code base for replicating our results under https://github.com/szegedai/MLSM.

papers.title: Data Processing Inequalities for the Quantum Guesswork
papers.abstract: Quantum guesswork has emerged as a crucial measure in assessing the distinguishability of nonorthogonal quantum states. In this paper, we review and compare previous definitions of the quantum guesswork, and establish the pre and post data processing inequalities (DPIs) that are relevant for the guessing problem. We also derive improved lower and upper bounds on the quantum guesswork in terms of the Shannon entropy and Holevo's information.

papers.title: CChatbot: Secure Lifecycle Management for Persistent Confidential Chatbots
papers.abstract: Chatbots are increasingly deployed in stateful workflows where conversations span multiple sessions maintain persistent conversation state. Protecting such systems requires more than confidential inference: conversation objects must be securely created, processed, stored, resumed, and isolated throughout their lifecycle. This paper presents CChatbot, a TEE-backed confidential chatbot architecture that models conversations as persistent security-sensitive objects governed by an explicit lifecycle. CChatbot combines confidential inference with secure lifecycle management, including ownership enforcement, protected persistence, integrity validation and controlled resumption. We implement CChatbot on an AMD SEV-SNP confidential virtual machine and an NVIDIA H100 confidential GPU. Our evaluation shows that lifecycle management adds only 1.7% overhead over confidential inference while secure create, store and resume operations remain lightweight. On a single-node deployment, CChatbot supports up to 512 concurrent users with affordable interaction latency.

papers.title: Asymptotic properties of k-means and its bias correction for high-dimension, low-sample-size data
papers.abstract: Although k-means is recognized as an effective method for analyzing high-dimension, low-sample-size (HDLSS) data, its asymptotic properties in such contexts remain underexplored. This study aims to deepen the understanding of k-means clustering under practical high-dimensional settings and investigates the asymptotic properties of k-means algorithms in case of HDLSS conditions. Based on the identified asymptotic properties of conventional k-means, a bias-corrected version of k-means was proposed and assessed for performance improvement. Additionally, in line with the current situation that kernel k-means lacks adequate theoretical exploration in high-dimensional environments, a theoretical analysis of kernel kmeans was conducted using a Gaussian kernel function for high-dimensional data, facilitating the theoretical comparison between kernel and standard k-means. Finally, numerical simulations were conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of both the methods, i.e., the proposed bias-corrected k-means and conventional k-means methods, including kernel k-means, in high-dimensional settings. Practitioners can leverage the bias-corrected k-means for more accurate clustering in high-dimensional contexts, improving data segmentation in fields ranging from bioinformatics to marketing analysis.

papers.title: Multi-dimensional hierarchical temporal alignment for improved temporal commonsense reasoning in large language models
papers.abstract: Benefiting from recent advances in generative AI and large language models (LLMs), current LLM-driven AI systems are rapidly reshaping how we reason, plan, and make decisions. Yet endowing these systems with human-like temporal intelligence (e.g., understanding and comparing events across time) remains largely unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Multi-dimensional Hierarchical Temporal Alignment framework (denoted as MHTA), of which the core idea is to effectively ground the temporal alignment of an LLM in both event-specific and cross-event real-world temporal commonsense knowledge. Specifically, we first frame the temporal space as a multi-dimensional hierarchical space, where each dimension comprises its own set of temporal units. Building on this formulation, we curate an initial burn-in dataset in which annotations are constructed to reflect real-world human temporal commonsense in accordance with our defined temporal space. Based on the initial burn-in dataset, we propose two complementary fine-tuning objectives: (i) Grounding the temporal alignment in event-specific temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved through a novel hierarchy-preserving Wasserstein loss, and (ii) Grounding the temporal alignment in cross-event temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved via a margin-adaptive triplet loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of MHTA, we conduct extensive experiments on three representative benchmarks (MCTACO, DurationQA, and TimeDial). For example, on the MCTACO dataset, MHTA improves Mistral-7B by 6.0% in accuracy and 10.3% in exact match, and improves DeepSeek-LLM-7B by 5.4% in accuracy and 9.8% in exact match. Combined with different backbones, MHTA surpasses nearly all baselines across the three benchmarks and exceeds the performance of advanced models such as GPT-4o on MCTACO and DurationQA. These results demonstrate that MHTA provides consistent gains in temporal commonsense reasoning across diverse LLM backbones.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Background: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously. Objectives: To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

papers.title: Necessity–Uncertainty Theory of Information: A Conceptual Framework
papers.abstract: Abstract: Information is often defined as the reduction of uncertainty. This paper argues that uncertainty alone does not fully explain the emergence or value of information. Necessity—the contextual demand to resolve uncertainty—must also be considered. By combining these two dimensions, we propose a simple formula: \[I = N \cdot U\] Here, \(U\) represents uncertainty measured through Shannon entropy, while \(N\) reflects the situational need for information on a scale from 0 to 1. The framework suggests that information arises, and matters, only when uncertainty exists and necessity requires resolution. Examples from communication, decision-making, and knowledge acquisition illustrate the theory’s relevance and practical scope. This framework extends Shannon’s theory by adding a human-centered dimension. It bridges mathematical information theory with epistemology and decision sciences. Everyday interactions—such as tutoring, communication, or decision-making—provide living evidence of the theory. Information is not merely an abstract reduction of entropy; it is the synthesis of uncertainty and necessity within real contexts of human inquiry. papers.title: Accelerating Discrete Diffusion Models for Combinatorial Optimization via Momentum Inference
papers.abstract: Neural network-based Combinatorial Optimization (CO) solvers are showing increasingly convincing performances on NP-complete (NPC) problems, alleviating the need for handcrafted heuristics. These methods are usually tested on problems with very informative features, such as coordinates in the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem. In this paper, we introduce D2CO-M, a discrete graph denoising diffusion model that learns how to efficiently generate high-quality solutions using an original momentum-based sampling inference strategy. The dynamics of traditional score-matching denoising diffusion can be interpreted as a stochastic gradient ascent guided by the Stein score, the gradient of the log-likelihood. D2CO-M shifts from this simple gradient ascent to a momentum-based sampling strategy fitted for discrete diffusion, inspired by fast momentum-enhanced first-order methods, as exploited in the Adam optimizer. We experiment with this momentum-based variant on two NP-hard optimization problems with complex fine-grained features: random Weighted Max-2-SAT instances, and real-world Cost Function Network instances describing Computational Protein Sequence Design problems, establishing D2CO-M as a competitive and robust tool for complex, real-world combinatorial optimization.

papers.title: Radio-Aware Clustering and Multi-Relay Routing for D2D-Assisted Hierarchical Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Existing hierarchical federated learning (HFL) schemes commonly form device clusters based on geographic or logical proximity, even though these criteria may poorly represent effective connectivity in industrial wireless environments. To address this, we propose RaLeD-FL, a radio-aware clustering framework for device-to-device HFL that jointly exploits direct and multi-relay device-to-device (D2D) paths. RaLeD-FL constructs a weighted connectivity graph by evaluating admissible paths according to their bottleneck capacity, end-to-end (E2E) reliability, cumulative delay, and hop count. Then, it combines Leiden community detection with multicriteria cluster-head selection, synchronization constraints, and lower and upper cluster-size controls. We evaluate RaLeD-FL using an ns-3/ns3-ai/Python co-simulation that incorporates industrial 5G connectivity, device mobility, and strongly non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. On MNIST dataset, RaLeD-FL reaches an accuracy of 0.95 twice faster than best-performing baselines and achieves a final accuracy of 0.98. On CIFAR-10 dataset, it is the only method that consistently exceeds 0.7 in accuracy. Compared with Edge-Vanilla, RaLeD-FL reduces E2E FL latency by 79 % on MNIST and 81% on CIFAR-10, while incurring a signaling overhead smaller than a single model update. These results suggest that radio-aware clustering and D2D multi-relay model-update routing can substantially improve the learning efficiency of HFL in industrial wireless environments.

papers.title: Towards Early and Accurate Disease Detection Through Multimodal Predictive Modeling: Fusion of Electronic Health Records, Medical Imaging, And Omics Data Using Interpretable Machine Learning.
papers.abstract: Early detection of disease is a cornerstone for improving patient outcomes, reducing costs, and enabling preventative interventions. Traditional predictive models often rely on a single type of data (e.g., imaging, clinical labs, or genomics). However, human health is inherently multimodal, involving a variety of data sources such as electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging, wearable sensor data, genomics, and clinical notes. Integrating these heterogeneous modalities into unified predictive modelsoffers a path to richer, more accurate, and more robust disease detection. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of methods in multimodal predictive modeling for early disease detection, illustrate architectural patterns and fusion strategies, discuss challenges (e.g. missing modalities, interpretability, generalizability, bias), and highlight promising directions. We also propose a reference architecture for developing such systems and suggest evaluation best practices.

papers.title: En-AgentSociety: Observable and Reproducible LLM-Based Urban Simulation at Regional Scale
papers.abstract: LLM-based urban simulators can generate semantically rich cityscale routines, but their outputs are difficult to inspect, reproduce, and validate. We present En-AgentSociety, short for Enhanced AgentSociety, an observable and fault-tolerant simulation platform built on top of AgentSociety. The system records prompts, responses, agent states, memories, emotions, visited places, POI categories, execution times, LLM latency, token usage, and generated trajectories. It also supports scalable regional map generation, traffic simulation integration, and direct export to mobility validation pipelines. In this demo, researchers can run regional simulations, inspect individual agent decisions through a web interface, debug unrealistic mobility behavior, resume failed runs, and compare generated traces against empirical mobility metrics. En-AgentSociety provides a transparent foundation for reproducible LLM-based urban simulation.

papers.title: AUDY: An Autonomous LLM-Driven AI Agent for Localized Automated Infrastructure Penetration Testing
papers.abstract: Abstract—The rapid expansion of IT infrastructure has dramatically expanded the cyberattack surface. Still, conventional manual penetration testing cannot keep up with continuous deployment cycles amid an ongoing cybersecurity skills gap. In this work, we present AUDY, a localized, autonomous LLM agent architecture for automated penetration testing and security reporting on infrastructure in native Bahasa Indonesia. Audy is based on the Mistral Small 3.2 24B base model and fine-tuned with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) on a domain-specific dataset of 4,934 cybersecurity samples. The agent executes within a standalone Kali Linux Docker container, as part of a decoupled reasoning-execution pipeline driven by the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and regulated by a two-layer safety control architecture that combines system instructions (SOUL.md) with a deterministic target-scope guardrail (_guard()). In the experiments, we find that QLoRA fine-tuning achieves a test token accuracy of 95.31% and a test loss of 0.1604 without overfitting. AUDY was successfully deployed in live tests against authorized institutional infrastructure, where it executed automated reconnaissance workflows strictly intercepting out-of-scope targets. Hardware evaluation on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell MIG instance shows that context window scaling up to 64K tokens remains within safe VRAM margins (94.96% usage). This study shows the promise of privacy-preserving, local LLM agents in democratizing cybersecurity assessments for low-resource languages.

papers.title: This Way Up: Evaluating Frequency–Elevation Mapping in Audio–Language Models
papers.abstract: In psychoacoustics, frequency-elevation mapping (FEM) refers to the widespread spatial connotation of auditory pitch: e.g., ascending and descending scales. We evaluate whether FEM is an emergent property in two deep learning models which are based on contrastive language-audio pretraining (CLAP): namely, MS-CLAP and LAION-CLAP. With MS-CLAP, the answer seems negative: after multiple attempts at prompt engineering, spatial elevation does not correlate with musical pitch in the TinySOL dataset of isolated notes from 14 instruments. The situation is different with LAION-CLAP, for which the prompt ``This sound source is located above my ears'' yields a surprisingly good zero-shot fundamental frequency estimator (Spearman's ρ=0.673). However, the same prompt yields chance-level performance in binary classification between environmental sounds which are typically placed above the listener (e.g., fireworks) versus below (e.g., pouring water into a glass). Together, these results suggest that FEM is not robustly or consistently available in the current generation of pretrained audio--language models. We attribute this shortcoming to a misalignment between the two encoders, rather than a limitation of the audio encoder on its own.

papers.title: Generating Linguistically Diverse and Semantically Faithful Patient Reports
papers.abstract: To protect patient privacy, medical models are frequently trained on synthetic datasets. Focusing on 13 clinical attributes commonly found in breast cancer records, we propose a synthetic data generation framework in which each generated sample is a data-report pair: the structured data capture the 13 attributes of interest, while the accompanying (French) text simulates a corresponding breast cancer pathology report. Data privacy and coverage are obtained by generating the structured data using a tabular data synthesiser. In this work, we focus on enhancing the diversity and quality of the generated texts through a combination of datadriven knowledge distillation, data filtering and data combination. Our findings suggest that the quality of the training data used for the student model outweighs its quantity; that combining data from multiple teachers helps improve performance; and that a compact model (Mistral 7B) can match the zero-shot Information Extraction performance of a significantly larger model (MedGemma 27B) when fine-tuned on high-quality synthetic data 1 .

papers.title: Socio-Technical Conflict and Adaptive Governance: Applying Agent-Based Modelling to Inter-Civilizational and Environmental Scenarios
papers.abstract: The paper is a thorough examination of socio-technical conflict and adaptive governance using agent-based modelling (ABM) that combines the computational simulation with the theory of systems and inter-civilizational literature. The research is inspired by the human-alien conflict analogy and uses analytical frameworks of heterogeneous agentsGEs of technologically and culturally distinct communities to support the impact of the combination of trust, information asymmetry, and adaptive policy patterns on the stability of the system and collaborative strengths. All emergent processes, including the formation of alliances, the process of policy adjustment, and conflict intensification, can be quantitatively studied in the proposed ABM framework where interactions vary in transparency, fidelity in communication, and flexibility on governance. Findings indicate that open information-exchange and evolving feedback systems are very effective in promoting trust and low entropy systemic states, which is typically achieved at equilibrium even in highly uncertain circumstances. On the other hand, there is cyclical instability and a possible breakdown of systems that are characterised by information opacy and stasis governance. The results highlight the importance of the structure of adaptive governance that is based on iterative learning, distributed decision-making, and real-time policy development that is vital to balance both in inter-civilizational and socio-ecological spheres. In addition to the astrobiological analogy, this research offers a conceptual and computational context on the reconsideration of governance in an epoch of mounting technological destabilization, environmental delicacy and world interdependence. The study provides a transdisciplinary template of designing next generations of governance systems that can sustain cooperation, reduce conflict, as well as create systemic stability across technological, ecological, and cultural boundaries because it reveals that the issue of resilience is not based on control, but rather on adaptatory coherence of agents.

papers.title: Logarithmic Adaptive Artificial Intelligence (LAAI): A Mathematical Modeling Framework for Dynamic Personalized Learning in Higher Education
papers.abstract: This study establishes the theoretical and computational foundation for Logarithmic Adaptive Artificial Intelligence (LAAI), an algorithmic framework designed to personalize instructional trajectories in higher education. The model formalizes student knowledge acquisition using a logarithmic progression, , capturing the natural phenomenon of diminishing marginal cognitive returns with respect to instructional duration. To continuously assess cognitive mastery, a multi-parameter composite knowledge index () is introduced, integrating response accuracy, item difficulty, error frequency, retry attempts, and latency. Based on this index, an adaptive engine dynamically recalibrates task difficulty and modulates instructional scaffolding. The core operational pipeline constitutes a closed-loop feedback architecture: Learner Task Response AI Diagnostics Knowledge Index Estimation Logarithmic Adaptation Successive Task Generation. The theoretical formulation is situated within contemporary literature on adaptive learning technologies, artificial intelligence in education (AIED), and human-centered design ethics. Methodological protocols for empirical validation, performance metrics, and inherent constraints are systematically outlined. Rather than relying on simulated datasets, this work establishes an analytical foundation intended for rigorous empirical testing.

papers.title: Le GENSA (GENeric Sensory Automaton): un modèle mathématique des interactions dynamiques par affinité en biologie
papers.abstract: This presentation revisits the paper 'The Generic Sensory Automaton (GENSA) for modeling affinity-based dynamics and interactions in biology', by Pastor et Thomas-Vaslin. In this talk, for further dissemination and exchanges, we present and discuss the GENSA (GENeric Sensory Automaton), a mathematical framework aimed at modeling biological systems, like the immune system. The GENSA is an automaton capable of detecting and responding to environmental changes and thus, capable of perceiving and responding to events in its surrounding. The capacity of the GENSA to detect events in its environment, and modify its state accordingly, is formalized through mathematical notions of specificity and sensitivity. We give and discuss two fundamental GENSAs: the Neyman-Pearson GENSA (NP-GENSA) and the Random Distortion Testing GENSA (RDT-GENSA). These two GENSAs embed distinct decision types and satisfy functional redundancy, in a sense close to the biological notion of degeneracy. We will present some prospects this model opens, especially with degeneracy. The possibility to construct networks of GENSAs and the perspectives these networks open will also be discussed, beyond the conclusions of the initial paper.

papers.title: Life Cipher reduced-round challenge: data for R = 4, 8, 12, 16 and 24
papers.abstract: Data for the Life Cipher reduced-round challenge: recover the key of any tier. The Life Cipher is an experimental authenticated cipher built on Conway's Game of Life on a 32 x 32 torus. Its specification, implementations and our own analysis are at https://github.com/t3spe/life-cipher (SPEC.md draft 0.4, algorithm version 1). Nothing about it is proven, and it must not protect real data. This challenge invites outside cryptanalysis. Each file is one tier: the recommended parameter set (T = 6,000, S = 16, k = 30) at R rounds per block, under its own secret key, a mined Game of Life configuration that passes the specification's vetting. Each file holds 1,024 messages. Each message is a random 128-byte IV, then the ciphertext of 1,024 all-zero blocks (131,072 bytes, so the keystream itself), then the 16-byte tag: 2^20 blocks of known plaintext per tier. papers.title: Contextbewuste Anomaliedetectie voor Complexe en Dynamische Industriële Omgevingen
papers.abstract: <!-- obsidian --> The explosion of Internet of Things (IoT) applications has significantly increased the availability of sequential data across virtually any domain in engineering and science, including industry, finance, environmental sciences, astronomy, and healthcare monitoring. This has led to massive collections of time series data, i.e., ordered sequences of observations measuring how one or more variables evolve over time. Given the scale of these collections, manual inspection is no longer feasible, and automated solutions have become a necessity. In this thesis, we focus on time series anomaly detection: the automatic identification of observations or events that deviate from regular patterns and do not conform to a well-defined notion of normal behaviour. Such anomalies can signal critical events, such as heart failures in cardiology, defects in jet turbine engineering, or ecosystem disturbances in earth sciences. Due to its practical importance, anomaly detection has been thoroughly investigated over the past five decades. Despite this intensive research, detecting contextual anomalies, observations that are anomalous only with respect to a specific context, remains a significant open challenge. Nevertheless, context is necessary to accurately detect anomalies in real-world applications, where 'normality' heavily relies on context. What constitutes an anomaly in one context may be considered normal in another. This dissertation investigates context-aware anomaly detection, a general methodology for injecting contextual information into anomaly detection models in an unsupervised manner. To this end, we define context as a partition of the feature space, a formulation that generalises over all existing interpretations of the concept. We then tackle context-aware anomaly detection from two complementary angles: the temporal context, a partition of the time domain into intervals of semantically meaningful behaviour, and the subspace context, a partition of the variable space into subsets of related attributes. For the temporal context, we propose PaTSS, a novel unsupervised method for time series semantic segmentation that explicitly models gradual state transitions between contexts. Building on this, SemSegAD leverages the identified temporal contexts to perform anomaly detection within each context independently, thereby lifting any existing anomaly detection model into a contextual setting without requiring additional supervision. We demonstrate that SemSegAD not only significantly outperforms existing contextual anomaly detection methods, but also consistently improves upon the performance of the underlying model. For the subspace context, we propose SubTSMD, a novel method for discovering motifs across variable-size subspaces of a multivariate time series, thereby identifying which groups of variables collectively define a meaningful context. Building on this, HydraAD exploits subspace structure through competing random convolutional kernels to achieve exceptionally fast and accurate anomaly detection.

papers.title: GraPEX: GRAdual Pattern EXplainer for multivariate time series classification
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series (MTS) classifiers, especially ensemble and Deep neural network models, have demonstrated strong performance in critical domains such as healthcare, predictive maintenance, and activity recognition. However, their black-box nature limits their adoption, as users cannot justify or understand the decisions they produce. Existing post-hoc explanation methods, whether based on feature attribution or counterfactual search, reduce explanations to numerical importance scores over individual time steps or variables and do not take into account the covariations that may exist between variables. In this paper, we introduce GRAPEX (GRAdual Pattern EXplainer for multivariate time series), a post-hoc, model-agnostic counterfactual explanation framework that leverages gradual patterns, which are co-variation rules in the form "the more X increases/decreases, the more Y decreases/increases'', to generate semantically grounded explanations for MTS classifiers. GRAPEX mines class-discriminative seasonal gradual patterns from the training set, then constructs a counterfactual by interpolating the instance to explain towards a nearest unlike neighbour, guided by the temporal regions where variables co-vary. We evaluate GRAPEX on subset of the UEA benchmark datasets against four state-of-the-art counterfactual methods: CoMTE, TSEvo, SETS, and CONFETTI, measuring validity, proximity, sparsity, and plausibility. Our results show that GRAPEX achieves competitive validity with better plausibility on the generated counterfactuals.

papers.title: Identification automatique de domaines de connaissances dans un dictionnaire universel du XVIIIe s.
papers.abstract: On se propose de présenter les résultats d’une recherche visant à l’identification et à la classification automatique de domaines de connaissances dans un dictionnaire universel du XVIIIe siècle.L’œuvre support des analyses est l’édition de 1743 du Dictionnaire Universel François & Latin (désormais, DUFLT) dit de Trévoux. Environ 20 % des articles héberge un ou plusieurs paragraphes associés à une marque de domaine (Pétrequin 2009, Turcan 2024) qui stipule de quelle science (astronomie ...), art (poësie ... forge...) ou métier (charron ...) relève le contenu. On est loin de la systématicité de l’Encyclopédie de Diderot et d’Alembert (1751-1772) où 83% environ des articles est pourvu d’une marque de domaine (données tirées de l’ARTFL et de l’ENCCRE). Notre objectif est de parvenir à une classification complète de l’ensemble des paragraphes du dictionnaire en leur affectant un ou plusieurs domaines de connaissance. Pour ce faire, nous développons une approche combinant grands modèles de langage (LLMs) et modèles de classification supervisée. On soulignera que la classification en domaines de connaissances a déjà fait l’objet de plusieurs études computationnelles sur l’Encyclopédie de Diderot & d’Alembert (Horton et al. 2009, Roe et al. 2016, Brenon et al. 2022), mais qu’aucune n’a été conduite à ce jour sur le DUFLT.Dans une première partie, nous présenterons les choix méthodologiques qui structurent notre démarche. Nous justifierons le choix du paragraphe comme unité de base de nos analyses, le regroupement des marques de domaine (simples : en termes de géographie ...; complexes : Terme de Botanique & de Pharmacie) en un nombre restreint de « macro-domaines ». Nous aborderons également les difficultés liées à l’hétérogénéité de ces marques et à la nature parfois pluri-/inter-disciplinaire de leurs contenus.Dans une seconde partie, nous décrirons le protocole expérimental mis en œuvre. À partir d’un ensemble de paragraphes initialement pourvus d’une ou plusieurs marques de domaine (que l’on aura retirées), nous sollicitons différents LLMs dans un cadre de classification few-shot afin de leur faire associer un ou plusieurs macro-domaines. Les prédictions sont ensuite évaluées par comparaison avec les annotations existantes. Cette phase permet d’identifier les configurations de prompts et les modèles les plus performants, et d’affiner progressivement les instructions fournies aux modèles. Les résultats préliminaires montrent qu’un des modèles testés (Gemini 3.5 Flash) atteint un F-score proche de 70 % sur un jeu d’évaluation encore limité à une cinquantaine de paragraphes. L’extension de ce jeu de test constitue une étape importante afin d’obtenir une mesure plus robuste des performances.Le meilleur modèle sera ensuite appliqué à un ensemble de paragraphes dépourvus de marque de domaine. Les annotations produites feront l’objet d’une validation et d’une correction manuelle, permettant la constitution d’un corpus de référence (gold standard). Ce corpus servira à l’entraînement d’un modèle de classification supervisée fondé sur une architecture Transformer de type encodeur, mieux adaptée à un déploiement à grande échelle sur l’ensemble du dictionnaire.Nous montrerons que cette approche progressive, associant annotation assistée par LLM et apprentissage supervisé, permet non seulement d’améliorer la couverture de l’annotation thématique du DUFLT, mais aussi d’ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives pour l’étude de l’organisation des savoirs dans les dictionnaires encyclopédiques du XVIIIe siècle.

papers.title: Bust a Shuffle! A Formal Privacy Analysis of Voting Protocols with Multi-Server Mix Nets (Full Version)
papers.abstract: Vote privacy is a fundamental property of secure e-voting protocols. This is usually accomplished using mix nets, which shuffle and thus anonymize the votes cast. To distribute trust regarding vote privacy, mix nets with multiple servers are often required, especially in high-stakes elections. Formal, computer-aided verification has become a well-established method for verifying whether e-voting protocols ensure vote privacy. Numerous studies in this field have significantly advanced our understanding of vote privacy. However, existing studies of e-voting protocols based on verifiable mix nets have a significant limitation: they idealize the mix net's functionality or consider only a single mix server that is fully trusted regarding vote privacy. While this is understandable given the limitations of existing verification tools, it restricts the class of protocols that can be accurately analyzed. Previous research shows that this abstraction can result in overlooked vote privacy attacks. To address this open research problem, we present the first formal fine-grained model of a mix net which allows us to consider an arbitrary number of mixers. Using the ProVerif tool, we applied this model to verify that the Helios protocol, its variants Belenios and BeleniosRF, and the Perfectly Private Audit Trail (PPAT) protocol all provide vote privacy when considering this more accurate modeling of multi-server mix nets.

papers.title: AI가 여행자에게 추천하는 식당, 정말 지금 영업 중일까요 (Define404 Report No. 007)
papers.abstract: Asks a web-search AI assistant (Claude Sonnet 5.5), as a traveler, to recommend five restaurants in each of 150 randomly sampled Korean municipalities, once in Korean and once in English (300 answers, 1,329 recommendations), and checks each recommendation against the Korean local government restaurant licensing registry. Pre-registered by repository commit 6dc92ad. Of 1,011 recommendations found in the registry, 13 (1.3%, 95% CI 0.6 to 2.0) were registered as closed, with no difference between Korean and English questions. However, 30.4% of recommendations for English questions could not be found in the registry versus 18.0% for Korean questions (paired difference 14.3 percentage points, 9.3 to 19.3). The closure rule was revised after collection (v1.1, address match required); v1.0 results are reported in an appendix. Korean edition is the version of record; translations included.

papers.title: GREMLIN — Finding What Machines Don't Tell You
papers.abstract: Passive RF diagnostics and machine-state inference at FAIR. A 10-minute show-and-tell at the European GNU Radio Days 2026, Rennes. GREMLIN explores how much can be learned about complex small- and large-scale infrastructure and technical systems from the emitted RF signals they already produce. The talk presents ongoing work at FAIR as part of the EU iRIS project, combining high-rate RF signal acquisition, modern C++/DSP, time-series replay and machine-learning-assisted inference to detect hidden states, anomalies and correlations across distributed equipment, using maintainable, software-defined instrumentation based on GNU Radio 4.0. papers.title: Multilingual Repair of Uncertain Speech Transcripts with Visual Cues
papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition can yield plausible but incorrect transcripts, particularly for short functional messages. We propose a multilingual repair interface that marks uncertain spans and offers alternative words, targeted audio replay and, where validated, pictograms. French and Spanish are the initial languages. A controlled listening study will compare top-one transcripts, text alternatives and optional visual feedback under matched recognition errors. Outcomes will focus on recovery of task-relevant meaning and the cost of unnecessary repairs, with language-specific pictogram coverage treated as a constraint rather than a success metric by itself.

papers.title: Quality Over Quantity: Evaluating Data Qualification for Low-Resource Text-to-Speech in Cuban Spanish and Sarawak Malay
papers.abstract: This paper investigates signal-based data qualification for finetuning F5-TTS models using two low-resource case studies: a single-speaker Cuban Spanish audiobook corpus and a twospeaker conversational Sarawak Malay corpus. Four acoustic indicators are combined into a corpus-specific composite score, and models are fine-tuned using the complete corpus, the topranked 80%, and the bottom-ranked 80%. Results show that the effects of data selection vary across corpora, evaluation conditions, and metrics. For Cuban Spanish, the top-ranked subset improves in-domain WER but not out-of-domain WER. For Sarawak Malay, proxy objective measures favour the filtered subsets, although their interpretation is limited by dialect and domain mismatch. MOS point estimates slightly favour the topranked subset for both languages, but the confidence intervals overlap. These findings suggest that signal-based ranking can support data qualification and corpus analysis, but its downstream benefits should be interpreted alongside data coverage and human evaluation.

papers.title: Designing Physics-Informed Quantum Simulations with Qubits and Qudits
papers.abstract: Simulating the real-time dynamics of interacting quantum systems is a long-standing challenge for classical computation. This thesis studies how quantum computers can address this challenge in three settings from nuclear and particle physics: collective neutrino oscillations, low-energy nuclear dynamics, and lattice gauge theories coupled to matter. We examine how the choice of encoding, simulation algorithm, and error-correction strategy affects the resources needed to simulate each system. For collective three-flavour neutrino oscillations, we develop qubit and qutrit circuits and implement them on superconducting quantum processors. We compare their gate requirements and sensitivity to noise, and show that error mitigation yields flavour probabilities in agreement with theoretical predictions for several time steps. For nuclear dynamics described by pionless effective field theory, we formulate the problem in first quantization and derive explicit resource estimates for product-formula and quantum-signal-processing algorithms. In the dilute regime relevant to nuclear scattering, first-quantized methods reduce both logical-qubit and gate requirements relative to second-quantized approaches. Among the methods considered, generalized quantum signal processing gives the lowest estimated gate cost. These time-evolution estimates suggest that low-energy nuclear scattering could be a candidate application for early fault-tolerant quantum computers. Finally, we investigate how the local symmetries of lattice gauge theories can provide part of the redundancy needed for quantum error correction, helping to reduce the additional encoding overhead. For ZN gauge theories with prime N encoded on N-level qudits, we show that Gauss's law defines a code protecting against bit-flip errors. We identify its logical operators with gauge-invariant observables and use them to derive a bosonic dual description. We then extend the construction to qubit encodings of ZN gauge theories with N a power of 2, where the constraints require stabilizers beyond the Pauli group, and show how these constraints can still be used for error correction and gauge fixing. This paves the way to more efficient encodings, and introduces new tools for the study of lattice gauge theories. Together, these results show how physical structure can guide the choice of encodings, algorithms, and error-correction schemes for more resource-efficient quantum simulation.

In the dilute regime relevant to nuclear scattering, first-quantized methods reduce both logical-qubit and gate requirements relative to second-quantized approaches. Among the methods considered, generalized quantum signal processing gives the lowest estimated gate cost. These time-evolution estimates suggest that low-energy nuclear scattering could be a candidate application for early fault-tolerant quantum computers. Finally, we investigate how the local symmetries of lattice gauge theories can provide part of the redundancy needed for quantum error correction, helping to reduce the additional encoding overhead. For ZN gauge theories with prime N encoded on N-level qudits, we show that Gauss's law defines a code protecting against bit-flip errors. We identify its logical operators with gauge-invariant observables and use them to derive a bosonic dual description. We then extend the construction to qubit encodings of ZN gauge theories with N a power of 2, where the constraints require stabilizers beyond the Pauli group, and show how these constraints can still be used for error correction and gauge fixing. This paves the way to more efficient encodings, and introduces new tools for the study of lattice gauge theories. Together, these results show how physical structure can guide the choice of encodings, algorithms, and error-correction schemes for more resource-efficient quantum simulation.

papers.title: Towards Semi-Automatic Benchmarking of Large Language Models for Self-Regulated Language Learning
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular personal assistants for language learning purposes. While exhibiting impressive capabilities on various Natural Language Processing tasks, including text summarisation, paraphrase generation, and question answering, their capacity to provide language learners with pedagogically adequate feedback is less clear. This is due, among other causes, to the lack of annotated data. In this paper, we describe a framework which aims at bridging this gap by (i) collecting manually annotated LLM-generated answers to learners' queries, and (ii) using this data to automatically characterise LLM skills along pedagogical dimensions with respect to a taxonomy of self-regulated LLM uses by language learners. This framework has been used to assess the ability of contemporary mainstream LLMs to generate pedagogically adequate answers to L2 French learners. Preliminary results on a small manually annotated dataset (N = 49) show that establishing a definitive assessment of these models remains elusive; rather, they reveal an absence of consensus among human experts when evaluating models.
